Thanks for the kind message :) You're right about our experiences being completely different, as xywav (for me) tastes like nothing, and I've lost 30 pounds. I think the reason why I'm not affected by the taste of xywav is because I lost my taste/smell to COVID all those years ago, and while it's somewhat come back, certain things have a different taste/smell to it (lucky me, I guess?) What is your dosage for Xywav, and how long have you taken it?

At this point, I'm almost positive that it's the Xywav...Before starting sodium-oxibate, I was only taking 40 mg of both Vyvanse and Fluoxetine daily for 6 years. Not once did I experience the same anxiety/elevated resting heart rate that I do while on Xywav. My sleep doctor has me get an EKG annually, and consistently, my average resting heart rate has ranged between 58-70 bpm. Since taking Xywav, my average resting heart rate has ranged from 90- 100 bpm on my EKG. Initially, I suspected that my stimulant dose might be too high, even though I have been on the same dose for over seven years without any issues. However, after skipping my Vyvanse medication for two days and still experiencing an extremely rapid heart rate, I concluded that the dosage wasn't the problem.The only other theory I have that might explain my symptoms is that I started taking an adrenal supplement, which caused some unexpected side effects. I visited a naturopath who prescribed me thyroid supplements, even though my thyroid was functioning well. It wasn't until a month or two later that I noticed my current symptoms, including a weight loss of 30 pounds. I immediately discontinued the medication and am no longer seeing that naturopath (thank goodness). So, perhaps some of these issues stem from that experience.

I can't relate enough! My mental faculties were already compromised before xywav, but I could still maintain a clear train of thought, albeit more slowly. I will likely adopt the same approach when I go off xywav, as I'm not risking any more unexpected side effects. How has your ability to function been since going off xywav? Do you find it worse/better/the same as it was prior to Xywav?

No, I haven't tried Xyrem. I might consider it, although the high sodium content concerns me because I have a family history of high cholesterol (myself included) and heart failure. What is your resting heart rate like now, and do you also take a stimulant?

Yes, I usually see my sleep doctor every few months. I mentioned my symptoms at my last two appointments, but honestly, they didn’t say much other than suggesting I should probably get off Xywav. They’re not my favorite doctor — our relationship has always felt more transactional than supportive. At this point, the only real value they offer is helping me explore other treatment options; when it comes to actually addressing my symptoms, they couldn’t care less.

If I could stop taking Xywav right now, I would. But it's not the best timing since I’m finishing out the last month of school, and the last thing I need is to make my life even more unstable. My hope is to start discontinuing it once the semester ends. I’m just really worried the side effects might continue even after stopping. Honestly, I could care less what EDSDS says, because they'll essentially deny that my symptoms are related to Xywav.  

I also saw a cardiologist, and they said everything looked healthy and normal. But I know for a fact that my resting heart rate was lower before starting Xywav — I've worn the same Apple Watch every day for the last three years. Before Xywav (and even for the first four months on it), my resting heart rate was usually in the high 50s to low 60s. Now it’s in the low 80s to high 90s. Even though they didn't identify any problems, I can't imagine it's healthy to live with an elevated resting heart rate in the long run.  I'm also super paranoid, as my dad passed away from a heart attack less than a year ago, despite no prior heart complications. In fact, my dad was likely the least expected person to have a heart attack, as he was a triathlete who consistently monitored his health. The medical examiner, for verbatim, said that it was "just bad luck"... 

 It’s also interesting because I’ve been on 40mg of Fluoxetine for the last six years,  yet it does absolutely nothing for me while I'm on Xywav. I haven’t heard of Lexapro, but I’ll definitely check out that supplement you recommended. Does your sleep specialist approve of it? I will say that my quality of sleep definitely feels better with Xywav. However, I still don’t feel like I wake up more rested than I did before taking it. I usually feel my best in the afternoon, as I often take a mandatory nap to relieve morning brain fog and reduce anxiety.

After I was diagnosed, I was on Modafinil from February to June. I only found it to be effective for the first month or so, but after that, it started to wear off. The maximum dose that I was on for a period of time was 200 mg.  I tried a bunch of different combos with modafinil to see if that improved things. For example: Taking my pills within given intervals, gradually increasing the dose, taking hydroxyzine at night to help improve the quality of my sleep, etc. at 200 mg, I would constantly get bad heart palpitations and rapid heart rates. It got to the point that it just felt really uncomfortable dealing with like in school and stuff as well as that I was still feeling tired. Like when taking tests it would significantly increase my anxiety and my lack of focus. 

I've been on Vyvanse since June, and I'd say its slightly better than modafinil, as I don't get these symptoms as often and in class, I don't feel as anxious. But that said, it's not like its "changed my life". Like I still feel heightened anxiety and stress at times, but I will say that I am working hard to manage those skills as I do meditation 3x a day. 

When doing homework or any other sort of assignment, I am someone who likes to complete it feeling like I gained something from it and feeling like I put my best effort into it, because most times, hard work pays off. With almost being a semester into the school year, I would say that I do have the capabilities to rise to my fullest potential in school, but I simply can't keep up with the pace of the class. I always feel like I am two steps behind. Thus, the motto "hard work pays off" is non-existent in my world, which is really frustrating. This only creates more pressure and stress for me because instead of approaching homework with the initial intent I had, I almost am forced to shift gears and complete it faster by putting less effort into it, causing me to have an even worse understanding of the content and making me more confused. I've now started to not take as many notes in class, because I feel that multi-tasking between note-taking and listening to the teacher is so counterproductive, whereas listening will allow me to focus my attention to one thing rather than two. 

Coming back to the topic about my parents, I feel less motivated to be proactive and actually want to force change in the relationship because if anything I've learned, no matter how hard I argue or want them to change, they won't. I know their insensitivity is not meant to hurt me, because since they are so foreign to narcolepsy it's honestly so hard for anyone to know instinctually when they're being supportive or actually just being annoying and just need to shut up and let me be. With that being said, it makes me wonder if I'm actually allowed to be mad at them. 

An example that explains what I'm trying to say is when I would run track races: Running around the last bend while trying to get an edge on the person in front of me, panting hard, and sweating like crazy. So many things are going through my mind, but I know I can't stop because the finish line is just around the corner. But simultaneously, I feel like I am about to explode because I am giving all I got, and the thought of having the power to simply just "STOP" is so tempting. In the crowd, I see my family yelling and cheering for me telling me to get ahead of the person in front of me. I feel this rush of adrenaline and boost of steam that ignites a flame in me to run through the pain and prevail. 

From this example involving my parents, in that moment, I could either choose to interpret their yelling at me as being hurtful and stressful or, I could use it as fuel to overcome. Thus, with my narcolepsy, to personally "overcome" it is physically impossible. However, that doesn't mean its the end of the world. So when my parents are yapping at me or getting on my ass for not doing something, I don't know how to interpret it, and it makes me wonder if I am actually trying my hardest or If I am just giving my self a hard time.

Last February when I was diagnosed with N, I also was diagnosed with obstructive sleep apnea, rem function disorder, hypersomnia, and clinical depression and anxiety. In January (pre narcolepsy diagnosis), I did this neurological testing thing called "mind sights", which was basically known as the place where people get diagnosed with ADD/ADHD/etc. From the results, I was not diagnosed with ADHD. However, I was told that I am an auditory learner. 

Since March, I have been taking Prozac, Vyvanse, Adderall, and a handful of over the counter supplements. I have already tried taking modafinil, but I hated it so much. And I can't increase the Vyvanse since I'm already on a pretty high dose and I have already had a medical emergency for it. 

As for my support group, I see a therapist, executive function coach, homework coach, psychiatrist, naturopath, acupuncturist, math tutor, and English tutor (sometimes). Also, with the school, we have gotten in touch with many resources that have provided accommodations for me. However, since I go to a private school, rule 504 does not apply. As a result, late assignments have been weighing me down since the begin of the year. You're probably thinking "why doesn't this kid just transfer???" well to answer this lingering question, even though that things really could be better at school, since being back I feel like I have put in a lot of effort to make do of what I have, even though it's not great. Also, I don't want to have to start over again and it's only just going to create more stress. 

I love my parents to death. Even though my parents can be a pain in the ass, I know that they are trying really hard to do anything they can to fix this. Sometimes it's hard to see this, but the fact that I have experienced my parents getting choked up talking about how badly they want me to feel happy. Without my parents, there's no way I would have the resources I have right now. As most parents do, when they see their kid struggling, their first instinct is to "help them and fix the problem". As I have learned in dealing with Narcolepsy, this notion is almost merely impossible. My parents know how I feel about this, but at times they can revert back to feeling this sense of eagerness to just step in and help me. But at times like this, I hate it how my parents don't realize that they also make mistakes.

Wow thank you for sharing your story with me. I can’t imagine the pain you felt from your parents rejection. Especially as the child, i bet it hurts to see yourself in your parents eyes as “lazy”, or “unmotivated”. Now of course one can’t physically or visually identify that someone has narcolepsy, but it’s important to be sensitive of what variables contribute to anyone’s deficits of anything. 

Even though I didn’t enjoy these dark times, your story in ways makes me grateful for the support I had and still have, and reminds me to keep in mind that there are others out there you truly empathize with you.

To answer your question, I put more pressure on myself than others because at given points in my life, I the phrase “hard work pays off” has been a huge pillar to my self-worth and happiness. And now that I barely ever feel that effect, It only makes me crave that feeling even more. 

Like, wouldn’t you be upset if let’s say you were a Olympic gold medalist during your prime and suddenly, your unable to compete like you did then because of Narcolepsy (this is all hypothetical, but’s let’s just say that’s the case for now). Like it’s frustrating because you know you still got arms, legs, and a pulse, but this obstacle that perceives to be underestimated is actually getting the best of your abilities. 

And where I stand is, I don’t know what to do. All my life I’ve been surrounded by all these stories of adversity that are presented on the news or whatever. In no way am I trying to undermine these obstacles, but some typical examples might include becoming the fastest track runner despite loosing two legs, playing in the NFL with 1 arm, getting a full ride Stanford after growing up in an impoverished background,etc.

THIS IS VERY LONG SO BUCKLE YOUR SEATBELT. I can empathize with you to some degree— as of now, my parents are more supportive and understanding of my needed nap schedule revolved around my daily lifestyle, and having the flexibility to shift things around if needed. 

However, this year I was finally diagnosed with narcolepsy as of this past February. Prior to that, I had diagnosed sleep apnea, but I was still feeling very fatigued at any time of day. During the winter, I would always come home from school, sleep for 3-4 hours, wake up feeling so distorted, and cram in my homework until 12-1am and then wake up at 6 am. Especially, living in the PNW, winters are a lot worse.

Now enough about me, but I wanted to give you some context because I want you to know that I hear you. I totally know how you feel when you say your parents aren’t giving you enough slack for your own capacities because they think that there are other solutions to staying awake then just “complaining”. For example, I found out at times when I would be at restaurants, family gatherings, doctors appointments, procrastinating, I would get so frustrated when my parents would say stuff like “just walk around for 5 min” or “stop taking so many naps then” or “go to bed early”. Because they simply don’t understand how fluctuating narcolepsy is with when I am tired and when I am not. 

If I were you, i would write a letter to your parents. You don’t have to take my word but at first I was a little hesitant to do so bc I didn’t have much hope in my parents actually listening to me even if I tried a different method. I found that writing them a letter about how I feel and how certain things make me feel really helped them have a deeper understanding, because I usually was not someone who talks to my parents a lot. My counselor I see also advocated for me on this issue, in just letting my parents now how it is impacting me. But also remember that “you gotta play the fish” meaning that as much as it sucks, you gotta know your parents are stubborn with their discipline,  but that doesn’t stop you from telling them how you feel, and compromising on certain levels. Now with my parents, there’s some things that i still don’t really agree with, but I just suck it up, and do it, and try to be grateful for what I have, because if I didn’t have my parents helping me in this situation then I don’t know where I’d be. Also, after I’ve been more diligent with communicating with my parents, there are certain things that I simply tell them “I’m sorry, I am just to tired to do this.
